title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

reading.body:
This incident describes a coordinated attempt to manipulate AI systems at the data-ingestion layer rather than at the point of model deployment. A fictitious organization produced a large volume of text designed to appear academically credible, with the explicit goal of influencing how AI chatbots retrieve and cite sources. The failure mode is not one internal to any AI model but rather a deliberate exploitation of a structural property of those models: that they tend to treat well-formatted, citation-heavy text as authoritative. The operation targeted the upstream information environment that AI systems draw on, meaning no safeguard within the chatbot itself would have been positioned to catch it.

Catching this kind of manipulation would have required source-verification checks applied before content enters training data or retrieval indexes, specifically checks for legal existence, named authorship, and organizational history. The volume of output, over 560,000 words in nine days, exceeds what any human editorial review at scale would typically flag without automated detection of anomalous publication rates or entity-verification failures. The platform used was reportedly built for exactly this purpose, meaning the vulnerability it exploited was known and commercialized before this instance came to light.

What is not established is whether any AI system's outputs were measurably altered by the operation, whether any chatbot provider was aware of the campaign, or whether the funding and organizational links described in the reporting have been confirmed by legal proceedings or official findings.

reports.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

summary:
# Summary

A fake American think tank called the Hanover Institute, funded by Israel, published over 560,000 words across 124 reports in nine days using a platform designed to optimize content for AI chatbots. The website, which does not exist as a legal entity and has no named staff, presented pro-Israel arguments on controversial topics including alleged war crimes, torture of prisoners, and starvation in Gaza. The reports were framed to appear academically rigorous with citations from legitimate organizations, but persistently used language that undermined criticism of Israel. The site was built on technology specifically meant to influence how chatbots like ChatGPT and Claude cite and reference sources.

The operation is part of a broader Israeli government campaign financed through tens of millions of dollars routed via European advertising company Havas Media. The campaign employed multiple contractors including firms run by former Trump digital director Brad Parscale. Israeli officials have expressed frustration that the expensive public diplomacy efforts have failed to improve Israel's standing in American public opinion, where support has significantly declined since 2022. Experts warn the operation demonstrates a new threat of foreign governments manipulating AI training data to shape information.
